finding: In macaque and spider monkey striate cortex, most cells were simple, complex or hypercomplex, as in the cat but with smaller receptive fields and greater sensitivity to orientation, and a few were colour coded; cells were grouped in two independent column systems, one for receptive-field orientation and one for eye preference (ocular dominance), and the simple, monocularly driven cells lay in and near layer IV (monkey).

Simultaneous recordings showed that lateral geniculate neurons connected monosynaptically to a simple cell with high probability when their receptive field lay over an elongated simple-cell subregion of the same (on or off) signature, and almost never otherwise, implying that the simple receptive field, and so orientation selectivity, is laid down at the first thalamocortical synapse (cat).

Cooling the visual cortex, which largely inactivated the cortical network but left geniculate synaptic input working, left the orientation tuning of visually evoked synaptic potentials in simple cells almost unaffected, in agreement with Hubel and Wiesel's proposal that orientation tuning arises from the arrangement of geniculate inputs (cat).

Two-photon calcium imaging at single-cell resolution showed that the centres of orientation pinwheels in visual cortex are highly ordered: neurons selective for different orientations are clearly segregated even at the very centre (cat).

Review: in monkeys, cells in visual areas 1 and 2 and in higher visual areas are segregated into three interdigitating subdivisions that differ in selectivity for colour, stereopsis, movement and orientation; the form and colour pathways derive mainly from the parvocellular and the depth and movement pathways from the magnocellular geniculate subdivisions, and human perceptual experiments are consistent with this division.

Review: a database of reported connections identifies 25 predominantly visual neocortical areas and 7 visual-association areas in the macaque, linked by 305 mostly reciprocal pathways; laminar connection patterns place them in a hierarchy of 10 cortical levels with multiple intertwined processing streams (monkey).

In PET of healthy young men, face matching and dot-location matching both activated lateral occipital cortex, whereas face matching alone activated an occipitotemporal region and location matching alone a lateral superior parietal region, evidence for separate ventral and dorsal extrastriate pathways for object recognition and spatial localization (human).

Review: proposes that the ventral stream of projections from striate to inferotemporal cortex plays the major role in the perceptual identification of objects, whereas the dorsal stream from striate to posterior parietal cortex mediates the sensorimotor transformations for visually guided actions directed at them.

A patient with a profound disorder in perceiving the shape, orientation and size of objects guided her hand and fingers strikingly accurately to the very objects whose qualities she failed to perceive, suggesting that the visual perception of object qualities and their use in controlling manual skills have distinct neural substrates (human).

Ibotenic acid lesions of the middle temporal area (MT) in rhesus monkeys caused striking elevations in thresholds for discriminating motion direction but little or no change in contrast thresholds, so activity in MT contributes selectively to motion perception (monkey).

In rhesus monkeys discriminating weak motion signals, the sensitivity of most MT neurons was very similar to the animal's psychophysical sensitivity, and single neurons typically accounted for both the absolute threshold and the shape of the psychometric function (monkey).

A patient with bilateral posterior brain damage showed a disturbance of movement vision in a rather pure form, with movement perception through hearing and touch intact; the authors attribute it to bilateral lesions of the lateral temporo-occipital cortex and underlying white matter, beyond primary visual cortex (human).

PET in normal subjects localized colour to area V4 in the lingual and fusiform gyri and visual motion to area V5 at the temporo-parieto-occipital junction, while V1 and V2 were active in all conditions, direct evidence that, as in the macaque, different prestriate areas are specialized for different attributes of vision (human).

fMRI found a region of the fusiform gyrus, in 12 of 15 subjects, that was more active for faces than for common objects and, in further tests, for intact than scrambled faces, faces than houses and faces than hands; the results rule out accounts based on attention, subordinate-level classification or animate forms, so the region is selectively involved in face perception (human).

Recording in the largest fMRI-identified face-selective region of two macaques, almost all (97%) visually responsive neurons were strongly face selective, indicating that a cortical area dedicated to face processing exists (monkey).

In macaque inferior temporal cortex, many neurons responded to virtually every stimulus, others were selective for shape, colour or texture over large receptive fields, and a separate population responded selectively to faces, depending on the configuration of facial features and tolerant of changes in size and position, most often deep in the superior temporal sulcus (monkey).

When monkeys attended to one of two stimuli inside the receptive field of a neuron in area V4 or inferior temporal cortex, the response to the unattended stimulus was dramatically reduced, whereas cells in striate cortex were unaffected by attention (monkey).

Brief microstimulation of frontal eye field sites, with currents below those that evoke saccades, enhanced the visual responses of V4 neurons whose receptive fields corresponded to the stimulated site, depending on the receptive-field stimulus and on competing stimuli, whereas stimulating non-corresponding sites could suppress V4 responses (monkey).
Per its title (PubMed lists no abstract): reports visual capacity in the hemianopic field after a restricted occipital ablation (human).

Phase-encoded retinotopic fMRI with cortical surface reconstruction precisely delineated the borders of human visual areas V1, V2, VP, V3 and V4 from the visual field sign, and showed that human visual areas give more weight to the centre of gaze than their monkey counterparts (human).

Review: much of human visual cortex is organized into visual field maps, identified with fMRI in medial occipital (V1, V2, V3), lateral occipital (LO-1, LO-2, hMT+), ventral occipital (hV4, VO-1, VO-2), dorsal occipital (V3A, V3B) and posterior parietal cortex (IPS-0 to IPS-4), and arranged in clusters.

In Braille readers blinded early in life, tactile discrimination tasks activated primary and secondary visual cortex, whereas sighted controls showed deactivation, and a simple tactile stimulus without discrimination activated visual areas in neither group (human).

In people blind from an early age, transient magnetic stimulation of occipital (visual) cortex induced errors in identifying Braille and embossed Roman letters and distorted tactile perceptions, whereas occipital stimulation did not affect tactile performance in sighted subjects (human).

In macaques made amblyopic by experimental strabismus or anisometropia early in life, cortical binocularity was reduced in all, and in the more severe amblyopes, visual cortex neurons driven by the amblyopic eye had substantially lower optimal spatial frequency and spatial resolution; these neuronal abnormalities alone did not explain the full range of visual deficits (monkey).

High-field fMRI during migraine visual aura in three subjects showed BOLD changes with at least eight characteristics of cortical spreading depression, starting in extrastriate area V3A and progressing slowly (about 3.5 mm/min) over occipital cortex in register with the retinotopy of the percept, strongly suggesting that an event such as spreading depression generates the aura (human).

Five patients had a progressive dementia heralded by disorders of higher visual function, eventually with alexia, agraphia, visual agnosia and components of Balint's and Gerstmann's syndromes, while memory, insight and judgement were relatively preserved until late; imaging showed predominant parieto-occipital atrophy in two, and the underlying pathology was unknown (human).

Fusiform and occipital cortex responded more to fearful than to neutral faces in healthy controls and in patients with hippocampal sclerosis, but not in patients with amygdala damage, although their visual areas were structurally intact, and the emotional response of the fusiform cortex was parametrically related to the extent of amygdala damage (human).

In mouse primary visual cortex, 4 days of monocular lid suture at postnatal day 28 caused a maximal loss of responses to the deprived eye, and these ocular dominance shifts occurred during a critical period between P19 and P32; binocular deprivation did not reduce responses, and plasticity involved both geniculocortical and intracortical connections, showing a competitive, correlation-based plasticity in the developing mouse visual cortex (mouse).

Disrupting one isoform of glutamic acid decarboxylase prevented the loss of responsiveness to a briefly deprived eye in developing mouse visual cortex without affecting synaptic plasticity in vitro, and enhancing fast intracortical inhibition with benzodiazepines restored the plasticity in vivo (mouse).

In GAD65-knockout mice of all ages, and in wild-type mice before their critical period, benzodiazepines unmasked plasticity to monocular deprivation, and enhancing GABA transmission early in life made knockout mice insensitive to monocular deprivation as adults, so a threshold level of inhibition may trigger the critical period, once in life (mouse).

Chondroitin sulphate proteoglycans became organized into perineuronal nets as the critical period ended, which dark rearing delayed, and after degrading them with chondroitinase-ABC in adult rats, monocular deprivation shifted ocular dominance toward the nondeprived eye, so the mature extracellular matrix inhibits experience-dependent plasticity (rat).

Recordings in anesthetized mice showed that V1 neurons, although their receptive fields are up to one or two orders of magnitude larger than in other species, are nearly as selective for orientation and spatial frequency, include simple and complex cells, and that putative inhibitory neurons are generally less selective (mouse).

In awake head-fixed mice, most V1 neurons more than doubled their visually evoked firing when the animal ran rather than stood still, without changes in spontaneous firing or stimulus selectivity, whereas responses in the lateral geniculate nucleus did not increase with locomotion (mouse).

Locomotion activated VIP-positive neurons in mouse V1 independently of visual stimulation, largely through nicotinic input from the basal forebrain; activating VIP neurons increased V1 visual responses in stationary mice, and damaging them abolished the enhancement of V1 responses by locomotion (mouse).

In mice running in a virtual environment, layer 2/3 neurons of primary visual cortex were strongly driven by locomotion and by mismatch between actual and expected visual flow, suggesting that visual cortex may use predictive coding to detect mismatches between predicted and actual visual feedback (mouse).

Layer 2/3 pyramidal neurons of mouse visual cortex, characterized in vivo and then tested for connections in vitro, connected at twice the rate when they shared an orientation preference than when their preferences were orthogonal, and at much higher rates when their responses to natural stimuli were similar, pointing to fine-scale subnetworks (mouse).

Pathway tracing with receptive-field mapping showed that mouse V1 projects to 15 cortical fields, at least nine of which hold complete maps of the visual hemifield and are distinct areas; of the areas on its lateral border only LM shares the vertical meridian with V1, suggesting that LM is homologous to V2 (mouse).

Review: anatomical and physiological studies have revealed a complex network of specialized higher-order areas in mouse visual cortex, a model for studying how information is transformed across distinct processing stages.

Unlike pyramidal cells, somatostatin-expressing inhibitory neurons in the superficial layers of mouse visual cortex responded more when the receptive-field surround was stimulated, because horizontal cortical axons preferentially excite them, and perturbing them showed that they contribute to the surround suppression of pyramidal cells (mouse).

Optogenetically activating PV+ interneurons in mouse V1 sharpened the orientation tuning and enhanced the direction selectivity of nearby neurons and improved the animals' orientation discrimination, whereas activating somatostatin or VIP interneurons had no significant effect on selectivity (mouse).

Anterograde tracing in rhesus monkeys found pontine projections from prelunate cortex (including areas V3, PO, DP and dorsal V4d) and the posterior parahippocampal gyrus, but none from ventral V4, area TEO or the inferior temporal gyrus, so corticopontine input to the cerebellum appears to come from extrastriate areas concerned mainly with visual spatial parameters, visual motion and the peripheral visual field rather than object identification and central vision (monkey).

After large HRP injections into the macaque pontine nuclei, labelled corticopontine cells, all layer V pyramidal cells, were densest in areas 4 and 6, whereas primary visual cortex (area 17) held only a few, restricted to the region representing the lower periphery of the visual field (monkey).

In mice traversing a virtual environment, nearly half of V1 neurons were driven by a weighted sum of visual speed and run speed, and the population predicted a combination of the two better than either alone, so mouse V1 takes part in integrating visual motion and locomotion during navigation (mouse).

In seven retinotopically identified mouse visual areas, layer 2/3 populations each encoded a distinct combination of spatial and temporal frequency, orientation and direction preferences, suggesting that separate groups of areas are specialized for motion-related and pattern-related computations, perhaps analogous to dorsal and ventral streams (mouse).

Review: koniocellular neurons form a third channel in the primate lateral geniculate nucleus; in macaques the middle pair of koniocellular layers relays short-wavelength cone input to the cytochrome-oxidase blobs of V1 and the dorsal pair relays low-acuity information to layer I of V1, and koniocellular neurons that innervate extrastriate cortex are likely to sustain some visual behaviours in the absence of V1.
